paragraphs: The last paper showed that the political saying we examined there does not require the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments to be wholly unconnected with each other. I shall now undertake to show something further. Unless these departments are connected and blended enough to give each a constitutional control over the others, the degree of separation that the maxim requires, as essential to a free government, can never be properly maintained in practice.

Everyone agrees that the powers properly belonging to one department ought not to be directly and completely administered by either of the others. It is equally clear that none of them ought to have, directly or indirectly, an overruling influence over the others in the administration of their respective powers. No one will deny that power is of an encroaching nature and that it ought to be effectively restrained from passing the limits assigned to it. Once we have distinguished in theory the several classes of power, as they may be legislative, executive, or judiciary by their nature, the next and most difficult task is to provide some practical security for each against invasion by the others. What this security ought to be is the great problem to be solved.

Will it be enough to mark the boundaries of these departments precisely in the constitution of the government, and to trust these parchment barriers against the encroaching spirit of power? This is the security that the framers of most of the American constitutions appear to have relied on principally. But experience assures us that the effectiveness of this provision has been greatly overrated, and that some more adequate defense is indispensably necessary for the weaker members of the government against the stronger. The legislative department is everywhere extending the sphere of its activity and drawing all power into its impetuous vortex.

The founders of our republics deserve so much credit for the wisdom they have shown that no task could be less pleasing than pointing out the errors they have fallen into. Respect for truth, however, obliges us to remark that they seem never for a moment to have turned their eyes away from one danger to liberty: the overgrown and all-grasping prerogative of a hereditary monarch, supported and fortified by a hereditary branch of the legislative authority. They seem never to have recalled the danger from legislative usurpations. By gathering all power into the same hands, these must lead to the same tyranny that executive usurpations threaten.

In a government where numerous and extensive prerogatives are placed in the hands of a hereditary monarch, the executive department is very justly regarded as the source of danger and is watched with all the jealousy that zeal for liberty ought to inspire. In a democracy, a multitude of people exercise the legislative functions in person. They are continually exposed, by their inability to deliberate regularly and to act in concert, to the ambitious intrigues of their chief executives, and tyranny may well be feared to spring up in that same quarter on some favorable occasion. But consider a representative republic. There the executive office is carefully limited in both the extent and the duration of its power. The legislative power is exercised by an assembly which, because of its supposed influence over the people, is filled with fearless confidence in its own strength. That assembly is numerous enough to feel all the passions that move a multitude, yet not so numerous as to be unable to pursue the objects of those passions by means that reason prescribes. It is against the enterprising ambition of this department that the people ought to direct all their jealousy and exhaust all their precautions.

The legislative department has a superiority in our governments for other reasons as well. Its constitutional powers are at once more extensive and less open to precise limits. It can therefore more easily mask, under complicated and indirect measures, the encroachments it makes on the coordinate departments. In legislative bodies it is not infrequently a question of real delicacy whether the operation of a particular measure will or will not reach beyond the legislative sphere. On the other side, the executive power is confined within a narrower compass and is simpler by its nature, and the judiciary is marked out by landmarks still less uncertain. Projects of usurpation by either of these departments would therefore immediately betray and defeat themselves. Nor is this all. The legislative department alone has access to the pockets of the people. In some constitutions it has full discretion, and in all it has a prevailing influence, over the pay of those who fill the other departments. This creates a dependence in the latter, which gives the legislature still greater ease in encroaching on them.

I have appealed to our own experience for the truth of what I say on this subject. If it were necessary to confirm this experience with particular proofs, they could be multiplied without end. I could find a witness in every citizen who has taken part in, or paid attention to, the course of public administrations. I could collect plentiful evidence from the records and archives of every State in the Union. But I will offer more concise evidence that is equally satisfactory: the example of two States, attested by two unexceptionable authorities.

The first example is that of Virginia, a State which, as we have seen, has expressly declared in its constitution that the three great departments ought not to be intermixed. The authority in support of it is Mr. Jefferson, who, besides his other advantages for observing how the government operates, was himself its chief executive. To convey fully the ideas his experience impressed on him in this matter, I must quote a passage of some length from his very interesting Notes on the State of Virginia, p. 195. "All the powers of government, legislative, executive, and judiciary, result to the legislative body. The concentrating these in the same hands, is precisely the definition of despotic government. It will be no alleviation, that these powers will be exercised by a plurality of hands, and not by a single one. One hundred and seventy-three despots would surely be as oppressive as one. Let those who doubt it, turn their eyes on the republic of Venice. As little will it avail us, that they are chosen by ourselves. An ELECTIVE DESPOTISM was not the government we fought for; but one which should not only be founded on free principles, but in which the powers of government should be so divided and balanced among several bodies of magistracy, as that no one could transcend their legal limits, without being effectually checked and restrained by the others. For this reason, that convention which passed the ordinance of government, laid its foundation on this basis, that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments should be separate and distinct, so that no person should exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time. BUT NO BARRIER WAS PROVIDED BETWEEN THESE SEVERAL POWERS. The judiciary and the executive members were left dependent on the legislative for their subsistence in office, and some of them for their continuance in it. If, therefore, the legislature assumes executive and judiciary powers, no opposition is likely to be made; nor, if made, can be effectual; because in that case they may put their proceedings into the form of acts of Assembly, which will render them obligatory on the other branches. They have accordingly, IN MANY instances, DECIDED RIGHTS which should have been left to JUDICIARY CONTROVERSY, and THE DIRECTION OF THE EXECUTIVE, DURING THE WHOLE TIME OF THEIR SESSION, IS BECOMING HABITUAL AND FAMILIAR."

The other State I shall take as an example is Pennsylvania, and the other authority is the Council of Censors, which met in the years 1783 and 1784. Part of this body's duty, as laid out by the constitution, was "to inquire whether the constitution had been preserved inviolate in every part; and whether the legislative and executive branches of government had performed their duty as guardians of the people, or assumed to themselves, or exercised, other or greater powers than they are entitled to by the constitution." In carrying out this trust, the council was necessarily led to compare both the legislative and the executive proceedings with the constitutional powers of these departments. From the facts it listed, most of which both sides in the council accepted as true, it appears that the legislature had flagrantly violated the constitution in a variety of important instances.

A great number of laws had been passed which violated, without any apparent necessity, the rule requiring that all bills of a public nature be printed beforehand for the people's consideration. This is one of the precautions the constitution relies on chiefly against improper acts of the legislature.
The constitutional trial by jury had been violated, and powers had been assumed that the constitution had not delegated.

The salaries of the judges, which the constitution expressly requires to be fixed, had been varied from time to time, and cases belonging to the judiciary department had frequently been drawn into legislative hearing and decision.

Those who wish to see the particulars under each of these heads may consult the journals of the council, which are in print. It will be found that some of them may be blamed on peculiar circumstances connected with the war, but that most of them may be regarded as the natural offshoots of an ill-constituted government.

It appears, also, that the executive department had not been innocent of frequent breaches of the constitution. Three observations ought to be made on this head, however. FIRST, a great proportion of the instances were either produced directly by the necessities of the war or recommended by Congress or the commander-in-chief. SECOND, in most of the other instances, they conformed to the declared or known views of the legislative department. THIRD, the executive department of Pennsylvania differs from that of the other States in the number of members composing it. In this respect it has as much kinship with a legislative assembly as with an executive council. It is at once exempt from the restraint of individual responsibility for the acts of the body, and it draws confidence from mutual example and joint influence. Unauthorized measures would therefore, of course, be hazarded more freely than where the executive department is administered by a single hand, or by a few hands.

The conclusion I am warranted in drawing from these observations is that a mere marking of the constitutional limits of the separate departments on parchment is not a sufficient guard against those encroachments which lead to a tyrannical concentration of all the powers of government in the same hands.
